newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil has serious police violence problem-report.
newsitem.headline: Brazil has serious police violence problem-report.

text.p: Brazil has one of the worst human rights records in South America and a serious problem with police violence, rights activists said on Thursday.

In its "World Report 1997," the non-governmental Human Rights Watch/Americas said there was a "striking contrast" between the human rights goals set out by Brazil's government and the serious violations that continued to occur.

"We are extremely concerned by the gravity and the variety of human rights violations which continue," James Cavallaro, the organisation's representative in Brazil, said. "Police violence is one of the worst human rights problems in Brazil."
He said the two "most worrisome" areas of police violence were in the states of Rio de Janeiro and Rio Grande do Norte.

Human Rights Watch blames an almost six-fold increase in civilian deaths at the hands of police in Rio on new policies that promote and financially reward police officers for acts of bravery. "The policies are at a minimum irresponsible, but may well be criminal policies," Cavallaro said.
In Rio Grande do Norte, Deputy Secretary of Public Security Maurilio Pinto de Medeiros continues in his position despite evidence of his supervision of a death squad, he said.

Human Rights Watch criticised the impunity of police officers involved in the 1992 massacre of 111 prisoners in Sao Paulo's Carandiru prison and the killing of 19 landless peasants in the Amazonian state of Para in April this year.

Cavallaro also deplored Congress' watering down of a law to transfer from military to ordinary courts jurisdiction over crimes committed by military police officers. The law is a key measure in the federal government's National Human Rights Plan announced in May and welcomed by human rights groups.

"Congress has failed consistently in the most grave manner to respond to the challenge presented by the human rights plan," he said. "In the area of public security Congress has not implemented a single measure (of the plan)."

But Cavallaro praised the federal government's positive attitude to combat human rights violations, as well as efforts by two states to reduce police violence. "The concrete programmes enacted in the states of Sao Paulo and Pernambuco and the open attitude of the federal government are the main highlights in the area of human rights in 1996," he said.
